text:
At three in the morning, someone brought Clara a sandwich and asked whether she had passed gas. The sandwich was wrapped in plastic bearing the words A FRESH APPROACH. The woman wore dark-blue scrubs and a cardigan with pearl buttons.

“I don’t know,” Clara said.

“Well, think about it.”

Beyond the curtain, a machine made a sound like a truck reversing.

“I may have.”

The woman checked a box.

“That’s good news.”

The sandwich contained turkey and a pale coin of tomato. Clara had not eaten turkey for eleven years. Her husband sometimes forgot this when buying groceries, which she considered a failure of imagination rather than memory.

She ate it in six bites.

Her daughter was not in the room.

For a moment this seemed unsurprising. Then it became the only fact in the room.

Clara pressed the call button. A red light appeared beside the door. There was something reassuring about having made a signal, even if no one answered.

The baby had been born at eleven seventeen. Clara remembered because Ben had announced the time in the voice he used when identifying a bird. There had been a furious face, dark hair, a hand opening against her collarbone. Someone had said, “A little girl.”

Later, a nurse had fitted the baby to Clara’s breast with the practical confidence of someone attaching a vacuum-cleaner accessory. Clara had felt grateful, then embarrassed by her gratitude.

Ben had gone home to feed the cat and bring a longer phone charger. Clara remembered encouraging him. She couldn’t remember why the charger had seemed important.

She pressed the button again.

“They don’t come faster if you keep doing it,” a woman said beyond the curtain.

“I’m sorry.”

“It isn’t me you’re bothering.”

The curtain moved. A woman stood holding a plastic water jug. Her hair was gathered into a disintegrating knot. She wore silver sandals.

“Did they take yours?” Clara asked.

“For the hearing.”

“What?”

“The hearing test.”

“Oh. How long ago?”

“Do you have the time?”

Clara found her phone beneath the sheet, hot and nearly dead.

“Three twenty-four.”

“That’s not what it is over there.”

The corridor clock read 2:08.

They considered this silently.

The woman’s name was Ruth. It appeared on a card beside her bed, above the words MY GOAL TODAY. Someone had written: Comfort.

“Is that your goal?” Clara asked.

“They asked me when I was still quite impressionable.”

A nurse appeared, pushing a cart.

“Pain?”

“Yes,” Ruth said.

“On a scale?”

“Must I?”

Clara asked about her daughter.

“Baby’s being checked.”

“Checked for what?”

“Just the checks.”

“When will she come back?”

The nurse consulted her screen.

“You’re twelve?”

“B,” Ruth supplied. “I’m A.”

“I’ll let them know you’re ready.”

After she left, Clara said, “I was already ready.”

“You have to tell them.”

***

Before the hospital, Clara had written website descriptions for a furniture-rental company: responsive seating, collaborative surfaces, storage that adapts to the way you work. During pregnancy she had become unable to write adaptable without feeling angry.

Her manager had offered her a cushion.

Near the end, familiar things sometimes appeared newly assembled. Ben washing a glass would look like an actor demonstrating the life she had chosen. Her obstetrician said pregnancy could produce a feeling of unreality.

“Is that hormonal?”

“Some of it.”

Now Clara lowered her feet to the floor.

“Are we allowed to walk around?”

“I’ve been doing it,” Ruth said.

The corridor smelled of disinfectant and warmed bread. Through one doorway, a woman wearing headphones held a baby and watched two men restore a house on television. In another, a man slept with his face pressed into a coat.

The nurses’ station was empty. Beside a bowl of peppermints stood a photograph of an infant beneath the words EVERY BABY IS OUR BABY.

A woman in a green robe was trying a locked door.

“Is that the nursery?” Clara asked.

“Supply closet.”

“Do you need something?”

“A towel.”

Her name was Esme. She had delivered twins. One was in intensive care; the other was “somewhere normal.”

“They keep asking which one I mean,” she said. “As though I’ve established preferences.”

Ruth offered her the water jug.

They walked to the window at the corridor’s end. Outside, a plastic bag caught on a pipe filled and emptied in the wind.

“I thought there would be more people,” Clara said.

“There were earlier,” Esme said.

Clara meant more people who appeared to know what was happening. She suspected they understood.

“Do you have children already?” she asked Ruth.

“One.”

“Where is he?”

“At school, usually.”

“No, I meant—”

“I know.”

Esme laughed and pressed her abdomen.

“Don’t.”

Somewhere a baby cried. All three turned.

“I can’t tell yet,” Clara said.

“Tell what?”

“Which one is mine.”

“Of course you can’t,” Ruth said. “You’ve just met.”

***

They found the nursery beyond doors marked AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY. A laundry bin propped one open.

Transparent bassinets stood in two rows. A radio played behind a partition. Clara recognized a tune her father had whistled while searching for parking.

A nurse sat eating yogurt.

“We’re looking for our babies,” Ruth said.

“Names?”

They gave their own.

“No, the babies’.”

“Mine doesn’t have one yet,” Clara said.

Ben wanted June. Clara liked it but disliked how pleased he had been to think of it.

“The surname, then.”

Clara gave hers, then Ben’s. They hadn’t settled that question. During labor, when someone asked, she had said, “Whatever’s easier.”

“Let’s see your bands.”

Clara held out her wrist. The printing on her pink bracelet had blurred where she had washed her hands.

“You’re twelve?”

“B.”

The nurse went behind the partition. Esme followed, asking something quietly.

Ruth walked between the bassinets. Clara stayed by the desk, embarrassed by the possibility of approaching the wrong baby.

The nearest was awake, regarding the air with great seriousness. Its card said BABY.

Clara waited for recognition. She had been told there would be a smell, a feeling, a knowledge older than thought. The baby moved beneath its blanket. She felt tenderness, but it wasn’t specific. She might have felt it for any small animal awake beneath fluorescent lights.

The nurse returned.

“This one.”

“Are you sure?”

“We check the bands.”

She lifted an ankle from the blanket and held its pink bracelet beside Clara’s.

“That’s you.”

Before Clara could read the numbers, the foot was tucked away.

“I’ll take you back.”

“What about hers?” Clara indicated Ruth.

“We’re sorting everybody out.”

Ruth raised a hand from the far end of the room.

***

Back in twelve B, the nurse placed the baby in Clara’s arms.

“Skin to skin. We’ll do the paperwork shortly.”

“What paperwork?”

“For discharge.”

“I thought tomorrow.”

“It is tomorrow.”

The baby’s head fitted beneath Clara’s chin. She smelled soap, warm cloth, something faintly metallic. The face seemed fuller than she remembered, less offended.

Ben didn’t answer. She sent: They’re saying we can go.

Ruth’s bed was empty. Her jug remained, its blue straw tilted toward the wall.

The baby opened its mouth against Clara’s gown. Feeding was difficult without the nurse. Clara tried to reproduce the arrangement of hands. The baby rooted, slipped, became angry. She apologized aloud.

At last it latched. The pain was astonishing.

“Oh,” she said.

It drank with a concentration that relieved her of any need to think.

A woman in a flowered blouse arrived with a clipboard. Clara should call if she developed a fever. Someone would visit, or she should arrange a visit. The baby needed six wet diapers, unless the woman had said seven.

“Do you feel safe at home?”

“Yes.”

“Do you have support?”

“My husband’s coming.”

“Lovely.”

Clara signed. Her middle initial was wrong on one page, but the woman had already turned it.

“Any questions?”

Clara had so many she couldn’t separate them.

“No.”

She received a bag of supplies and a booklet called YOUR NEW BEGINNING. Its cover showed two hands enclosing a smaller hand. None appeared to belong to anyone recently in pain.

***

Ben still didn’t answer. His absence became strangely agreeable. Clara pictured his phone vibrating on the kitchen counter while the cat watched. She felt temporarily excused from explaining herself.

She dressed slowly, putting the baby down, picking it up when it cried.

In her bag was the yellow outfit they had bought together. Ben had held it up in the shop.

“Imagine there being someone in this.”

She had tried, but always pictured a doll.

Now there was someone.

The baby objected to the sleeves. Clara waited, then tried again. She had never performed an ordinary task with such attention.

A young nurse came to remove the electronic ankle tag.

“Heading out?”

“I think so. Is there anything else?”

“Downstairs will get you.”

She cut off Clara’s pink bracelet too.

In the corridor, Esme sat beside the supply closet holding a folded towel.

“Did you find them?” Clara asked.

“One at a time.”

“I’m going home.”

“So I see.”

Clara wanted to offer reassurance, but couldn’t think what to say.

Esme touched the yellow sleeve with one finger.

“Nice.”

***

Downstairs, a man at reception was applying hand cream. He asked whether Clara had a ride.

“I’ll get a taxi.”

“Car seat?”

Then she remembered: Ben’s car, the instructional videos, his triumphant demonstration of the click.

“My husband has it. He’s coming.”

She sat near the doors. Outside, rain fell with the persistence of something begun long before anyone noticed.

Her phone lit up.

Coming now. Fell asleep. So sorry. How’s our girl?

She watched until the screen darkened.

She hadn’t changed the baby’s diaper. This struck her as a failure requiring immediate correction. She carried the baby into a family bathroom.

In the long mirror she saw a woman with a shopping bag, a badly buttoned coat, a yellow bundle. For a second she thought someone else had entered.

She lowered the changing table. The snaps were difficult. She opened them one by one while the baby watched the ceiling.

There was no ambiguity once the diaper was open.

Her daughter had been a girl. This was a boy.

Clara stood still.

She remembered the announcement, Ben crying, the small body lifted toward her. Nothing in that memory had the quality of a dream.

The boy kicked. Urine arced onto the yellow outfit.

“Oh, sweetheart.”

She slid a clean diaper beneath him, wiped his skin, fastened the tabs. Her hands knew what to do, having been shown once.

Then she sat with him against her chest.

Beyond the wall, the lobby continued: cart wheels, elevator chimes. She could tell the man at reception. He would stop rubbing cream into his hands. Calls would be made. Somewhere upstairs, another woman would be waiting, asleep, or insisting she had been ready all along.

Clara tried to picture her daughter. Dark hair, furious mouth. She could retrieve the features, but they wouldn’t assemble into a face.

The boy’s face was before her. A scratch marked his cheek. His upper lip trembled.

She knew he wasn’t hers. She wasn’t confused now.

Her phone vibrated. Ben was probably at a red light, ashamed and eager, preparing to become useful.

Clara laughed quietly. She waited for the laughter to become something else. It didn’t. An immense happiness had opened in her without permission. She felt it in her sore body, her hands supporting the boy, her feet on the tiles.

She kissed his scratched cheek.

When Ben called again, she answered.

“Where are you?”

“Downstairs.”

“I’m outside. Need me to come in?”

She looked at the damp outfit. She could change him at home.

“No. We’re coming.”

She stood carefully. The boy stirred and settled. At the door she shifted him higher against her shoulder, turned the lock, and carried him out.
